teaser: She has no myth to hide behind. That was enough to bring Goya before the Inquisition.
review_notes:
Dimensions given as about 97 x 190 cm (Prado).
Godoy inventory of 1800 (visit of Pedro Gonzalez de Sepulveda) as first record; Rokeby Venus entering Godoy's collection later.
Inquisition summons of 1815 with no surviving record of Goya's answer.
Story that the clothed version covered the nude with a mechanism is tradition, presented as such.
1930 Spanish stamps and US postal refusal of mail bearing them: widely repeated, please verify.
Prado dates the work 1795-1800; catalog year 1800 kept.

lesson.text: The canvas is about 97 centimeters high and 190 wide, a little over 6 feet across. That is close to the length of a real bed. Goya painted this woman at roughly life size, so whoever stood in front of her met a body on the same scale as their own.

In Spain around 1800, that was dangerous. The Church frowned on painted nudes, and the Inquisition, the religious court that hunted heresy and indecency, could seize them. The few nudes that existed were goddesses or nymphs, kept in private rooms. A story from mythology was the excuse that made bare skin acceptable.
Goya removed the excuse. No Venus, no Cupid, no mirror, no cloud: only a woman of his own time, on a modern couch, who knows you are there.

Nobody knows who commissioned her for certain, but she first appears in 1800 in the collection of Manuel Godoy, the prime minister and the most powerful man in Spain after the king. He kept her in a private cabinet reserved for nudes, a room only chosen guests could enter.
Godoy's cabinet later also held the “Rokeby Venus” by Velázquez, the other great nude of Spanish painting. That Venus turns her back to the viewer. Goya's woman does the opposite.
What makes her so different from the goddesses? Much of the answer sits in three places: her face, the way her arms are placed, and what she is lying on.

lesson.title: No goddess
lesson.text: Three details that turn a nude into a person.

spots.title: The stare
spots.text: Flushed cheeks, dark eyes aimed straight at you, a hint of a smile. She is not caught by surprise and she is not ashamed. Earlier nudes usually look away or sleep.

spots.title: Arms behind the head
spots.text: Both hands are tucked behind her curls. Nothing shields the body. The pose is chosen, almost a challenge, and it pushes the torso toward the viewer.

spots.title: Pillows and lace
spots.text: The lace edges are flicked in with quick strokes of white and gray. These are fashionable household linens of Goya's day, not the timeless drapery of a myth.

lesson.text: Many viewers feel that the head sits a little oddly on the shoulders, as if it had been set onto the body afterward. That impression has fed two centuries of guessing. Was the face changed to protect someone? The Duchess of Alba, a friend of Goya, is the legendary candidate. Pepita Tudó, Godoy's mistress, is the one historians find more likely. No document settles it.

Goya then painted her a second time, in the same pose and at the same size, but dressed. The two canvases are known as the naked maja and the clothed maja. A maja was a stylish, sharp-tongued young woman of working-class Madrid, although that name was only attached to the pictures later.

Tradition says the clothed version hung in front of the nude one and could be moved aside to reveal her to trusted visitors. No mechanism survives, but the matching sizes make the story hard to resist.
Goya built the picture with very few elements, and the body does almost all the work. Its direction across the canvas is what gives the image its tension.
Follow how the figure is laid across the rectangle.

lines.label: A rising diagonal
lines.text: From the feet at lower left to the face at upper right, the body climbs through the picture. Your eye travels up it and ends on her eyes.

lines.label: Dark green behind
lines.text: The green velvet of the couch wraps the pale skin like a shadow. Against it, and against the bare brown wall, the body is the brightest thing in the room.

lines.label: The white bed
lines.text: Sheet and pillows form a long pale platform. Their cool whites make the warm, rosy flesh tones look even more alive.

lesson.text: When Godoy fell from power in 1808, his collection was seized. A few years later the Inquisition found the two paintings, judged them obscene, and in 1815 summoned Goya to say who had ordered them and why. No record of his answer survives. He kept his post as court painter.

The nude then spent most of the 19th century out of public view, in a back room of the Academy of San Fernando in Madrid. She entered the Prado only in 1901. Today the two versions hang side by side, and visitors do what Godoy's guests did: look from one to the other.
In 1930 Spain printed her on postage stamps to honor Goya. The United States postal service reportedly refused to deliver letters that carried them.

quiz.question: What made this nude so unusual for its time?
options: It shows a contemporary woman with no mythological story
It was the first oil painting made in Spain
quiz.explanation: There is no Venus or nymph here, only a woman of Goya's own day.

quiz.question: In whose collection does the painting first appear, in 1800?
quiz.explanation: Godoy kept it in a private cabinet reserved for nudes.

quiz.question: What did the Inquisition do in 1815?
options: It bought the painting for a church
It summoned Goya to explain who had ordered it
quiz.explanation: Goya was called to account, and no record of his answer survives.

quiz.question: How does the body cross the canvas?
options: Along a rising diagonal from the feet to the face
In a circle around the pillows
quiz.explanation: The figure climbs from lower left to upper right, ending at her eyes.

quiz.question: What is the companion picture Goya painted afterward?
options: The same woman seen from behind
The same woman in the same pose, dressed
quiz.explanation: The clothed maja repeats the pose and the size.

facts.text: The woman in the painting is presented as the goddess Venus.
facts.explanation: Goya gave her no mythological disguise at all.

facts.text: The painting entered the Prado only in 1901.
facts.explanation: Before that it was kept out of public view at the Academy of San Fernando.

facts.text: Historians know for certain that the model was the Duchess of Alba.
facts.explanation: That is a legend; the model's identity has never been proven.
